strengths: Addresses an important and under-discussed issue: distributional symmetry breaking can materially affect when augmentation/equivariance helps, even when labels are invariant.
Proposes a simple, practical classifier-based diagnostic that is easy to interpret and apply across heterogeneous data types where hand-designed kernels are awkward.
The paper combines theory, synthetic validation, and empirical analysis across several relevant benchmarks, including MNIST, ModelNet40, QM9, QM7b, rMD17, OC20, and an LLM materials dataset.
The empirical observation that many common point-cloud/materials datasets are highly canonicalized is interesting and potentially useful for the equivariant-learning community.
The ridge-regression analysis gives a concrete mechanism by which invariant training or augmentation can hurt under data asymmetry, adding useful nuance to prior positive results on equivariance.
Appendices provide substantial experimental detail, sanity checks, architecture ablations for the task-independent metric, and comparisons to MMD-style alternatives.
weaknesses: The proposed metric is essentially a neural two-sample classifier accuracy, so its novelty is limited; much of its behavior depends on classifier class, optimization, sample size, and train/test construction rather than being an intrinsic property of the distribution.

The central practical question, when augmentation or equivariant modeling will help, remains only partially answered. The paper itself finds contradictory behavior across ModelNet40/MNIST versus QM9/QM7b, and the proposed task-dependent metric is reported as inconclusive and architecture-sensitive on key datasets.

The theoretical results are restricted to linear Gaussian ridge regression with stylized covariance structure. They are valuable but only loosely connected to the deep architectures and molecular/point-cloud settings used empirically.

Several empirical comparisons are not fully convincing as model-comparison evidence: some baselines are not state of the art, parameter counts and inductive biases differ, and results are often reported as single best/minimum test values rather than with enough seeds, confidence intervals, or validation-protocol detail.

The interpretation of high classifier accuracy as degree of canonicalization can be overstated, especially for infinite groups and datasets with obvious preprocessing artifacts such as aligned slabs or canonical molecular orientations.

The task-dependent extension relies on learning or choosing a canonicalization map, has acknowledged issues with self-symmetry, overfitting, and architecture sensitivity, and is not yet a reliable diagnostic.

Reproducibility is reasonable in spirit, but the manuscript depends on supplemental code and many dataset-specific pipelines; the main paper does not make all splits, seeds, and hyperparameter-selection criteria sufficiently transparent.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and under-discussed issue: datasets used with equivariant methods may be highly non-uniform over group orbits, so augmentation/equivariance assumptions should be checked rather than taken for granted.

The classifier two-sample test is simple, practical, and interpretable, and the paper applies it to a reasonably broad set of datasets including MNIST, ModelNet40, QM9/QM7b, rMD17, OC20, and a materials-language dataset.
The paper contains a nontrivial theoretical component on invariant ridge regression under asymmetric covariances, showing cases where augmentation or symmetrization can hurt despite invariant labels.

The empirical observation that many molecular and point-cloud benchmarks are strongly canonicalized is useful, and the local-QM9 analysis is an interesting attempt to explain why equivariant methods may still help on canonicalized molecular datasets.
weaknesses: The central methodological contribution is weak: a classifier two-sample test is a standard tool, and the paper mostly repackages it as a symmetry-breaking metric. The novelty relative to existing two-sample tests and prior symmetry-detection work is limited.

The proposed quantity is called a metric but is not a metric in the mathematical sense and is strongly dependent on classifier architecture, optimization, sample size, train/test split, and calibration. Accuracy values are not directly comparable across datasets or groups without stronger statistical controls.

The main empirical story is inconclusive. The paper finds high distributional symmetry breaking everywhere, but augmentation hurts on MNIST/ModelNet40 and helps on QM9/QM7b. The proposed task-independent metric therefore does not predict the practical question posed in the title: whether to augment.

The task-dependent metric, which should address the key failure mode of the task-independent metric, is admitted to be inconclusive on real datasets and sensitive to architecture. This leaves the paper without a reliable decision rule for augmentation.

The evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for a top-tier acceptance. Baselines and model choices appear uneven across domains, many results rely on generic architectures rather than carefully tuned competitive baselines, and uncertainty over seeds/splits is limited or absent for several headline comparisons.

Several findings may be obvious consequences of dataset preprocessing rather than substantive discoveries. For example, aligned CAD models, CORINA-generated molecular coordinates, and OC20 slabs aligned to the xy-plane are expected to be orientation-biased; the paper does not always separate trivial preprocessing artifacts from meaningful distributional structure.

The theory is technically interesting but disconnected from the empirical contribution. Linear Gaussian ridge regression with carefully structured covariance does not substantially validate the classifier metric, nor does it explain the mixed deep-learning results on molecular and point-cloud benchmarks.

Claims are often stronger than the evidence. The paper suggests rethinking symmetry biases and diagnosing when equivariance works, but the actual evidence mostly shows that canonicalization exists and that its relationship to augmentation performance remains unresolved.

Reproducibility details are scattered through a long appendix, and it is unclear whether code, trained models, exact preprocessing scripts, and hyperparameter search protocols are available. This is especially problematic because the proposed metric is implementation-sensitive.

strengths: The paper asks an important and underexplored question: when symmetry-aware learning helps depends not only on label equivariance/invariance but also on whether the input distribution itself is symmetric. This framing is timely and relevant to equivariant learning, data augmentation, point-cloud learning, and scientific ML.

The proposed classifier-based diagnostic for distributional symmetry breaking is simple, interpretable, broadly applicable, and practically useful. It avoids hand-designing domain-specific kernels and is validated with sensible sanity checks such as MNIST, synthetically rotated fractions, and artificially canonicalized/rotated datasets.

The empirical finding that several widely used point-cloud and molecular benchmarks are highly canonicalized is interesting and potentially impactful. The paper covers a broad range of datasets, including MNIST, ModelNet40, QM9, QM7b, rMD17, OC20, and a molecular-text/LLM setting.

The theory section adds substance beyond a purely empirical diagnostic paper. The ridge-regression analysis gives useful intuition for why invariant or augmented methods can help or hurt under data asymmetry, including under- and over-parameterized regimes.

The paper is intellectually honest about surprising results: despite high canonicalization in QM9/QM7b, augmentation and equivariant models often still help. The follow-up task-dependent and locality analyses are thoughtful and point toward plausible mechanisms rather than overclaiming a simple story.

The appendix is extensive and includes many implementation details, ablations, additional datasets, and comparisons to MMD-style alternatives, which improves reproducibility and confidence in the empirical observations.
weaknesses: The central practical implication remains only partially resolved. The task-independent metric reliably detects distributional asymmetry, but it does not consistently predict whether augmentation or equivariance will help; the authors themselves report that the behavior differs sharply between ModelNet40/MNIST and QM9/QM7b.

The classifier accuracy is called a metric, but it is architecture-, optimization-, sample-size-, and split-dependent. Although some ablations are provided, the paper would be stronger with clearer statistical calibration, uncertainty estimates across seeds/datasets, and more formal guidance on choosing classifier capacity.

The task-dependent metric is promising but immature. It is reported as inconclusive on important real datasets and highly sensitive to architecture choices, which weakens the paper’s ability to answer the motivating question of when to augment.

The theoretical contribution, while interesting, is limited to linear/ridge regression under Gaussian assumptions and stylized covariance structures. Its connection to the nonlinear equivariant architectures used in the experiments is suggestive rather than direct.

Some experimental comparisons are difficult to interpret as evidence about equivariance versus other factors. Models differ in architecture, optimization, parameterization, and group averaging strategy; stronger matched-capacity and matched-training comparisons would make the conclusions more convincing.

The empirical section is broad but somewhat exploratory. Several claims about causes of canonicalization, such as CORINA alignment or simulation initial conditions, are plausible but not always directly verified.

The paper could better position novelty relative to existing two-sample classifier tests and prior distributional symmetry tests. The main methodological novelty is adaptation and use in symmetry diagnostics rather than a fundamentally new statistical test.

The manuscript is long and dense, with many key caveats and important experimental details deferred to the appendix. The main narrative would benefit from sharper separation between established conclusions and hypotheses for future work.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and under-discussed issue: distributional symmetry breaking can make standard symmetry-aware methods, including augmentation and equivariant architectures, behave differently from what invariant-label arguments alone would suggest.

The proposed classifier-based diagnostic is simple, flexible across data modalities, and practically interpretable as a held-out distinguishability score between original and randomly augmented distributions.

The empirical survey is broad and interesting, covering MNIST, ModelNet40, QM9, QM7b, rMD17, OC20, and an LLM materials dataset, and it surfaces useful evidence that several common benchmarks are highly canonicalized or aligned.
The paper goes beyond diagnosis by studying downstream consequences of augmentation/equivariance and by proposing a task-dependent metric to explain when symmetry bias is label-useful.

The theoretical section provides a nontrivial analysis of invariant ridge regression under asymmetric covariances, giving useful intuition for why augmentation can help or hurt even when labels are invariant.
The appendices contain substantial experimental detail, ablations, and additional sanity checks, which improves reproducibility relative to many papers of similar scope.
weaknesses: The main metric is not really a metric in the mathematical sense and depends strongly on classifier architecture, optimization, sample size, and train/test construction. The paper discusses this but does not fully characterize calibration, confidence intervals, or failure modes under limited classifier capacity.

The novelty of using a classifier two-sample test is moderate; the paper’s contribution is more in applying it to symmetry breaking than in the diagnostic itself. Positioning against existing two-sample and invariance tests could be sharper.

The task-dependent metric is ad hoc and less mature than the task-independent diagnostic. It relies on a learned or random canonicalization network, has unclear thresholds, and may overfit or encode object identity for continuous groups, as the authors partly acknowledge.

The downstream empirical conclusions are suggestive but not fully decisive. Architecture, optimization budget, augmentation protocol, and equivariant/non-equivariant model capacity are not always controlled tightly enough to isolate the causal role of distributional symmetry breaking.

Some benchmark findings, such as ModelNet40 alignment or slab alignment in OC20, are unsurprising given dataset construction. The paper would be stronger with more cases where the diagnostic reveals genuinely hidden bias and then predicts a downstream decision prospectively.

The theory is technically interesting but narrow: linear ridge regression with stylized covariance assumptions only partially supports claims about modern equivariant neural networks, message passing, and local geometric features.
The practical decision flowchart is appealing but currently under-validated; there is no robust empirical threshold for when m(p_X) or t(p_X,Y) should change a practitioner’s augmentation choice.

The paper is long and somewhat diffuse, with many datasets, metrics, and hypotheses. The central narrative would benefit from tighter prioritization and clearer separation between established conclusions and exploratory observations.

strengths: The paper studies an important and under-discussed issue: distributional symmetry breaking can affect the value of equivariant architectures and data augmentation even when labels are invariant.
The proposed classifier-based diagnostic is simple, interpretable, easy to apply across modalities, and empirically reveals substantial canonicalization in several widely used datasets.
The paper combines several useful ingredients: synthetic sanity checks, real benchmark analyses, a task-dependent diagnostic, locality experiments, and theoretical ridge-regression results.

The theoretical section gives some concrete mechanisms by which augmentation or symmetrization can help or hurt under asymmetric data distributions, which adds depth beyond a purely empirical observation.
The writing is generally clear, and the paper is ambitious in connecting equivariant learning, augmentation, dataset bias, and benchmark practice.
weaknesses: The main metric is essentially a classifier two-sample test applied to original versus augmented data; this is useful, but the methodological novelty is limited and heavily dependent on classifier architecture, optimization, sample size, and calibration.

The paper sometimes treats classifier accuracy as a quantitative cross-dataset measure of symmetry breaking, but accuracy is not an intrinsic distributional distance and can be hard to compare across datasets, groups, architectures, and data complexities.

The empirical story is not fully convincing: high symmetry-breaking is found in many datasets, but augmentation/equivariance often still helps, so the headline implication for when to augment remains weak and partly post-hoc.

The task-dependent metric is ad hoc and insufficiently validated. It relies on an untrained equivariant network as a canonicalization proxy, and the paper does not establish robust thresholds or reliable decision rules despite presenting a practical flowchart.

Several downstream evaluations are not competitive benchmark studies, and the paper explicitly does not aim for SOTA. This weakens claims about practical implications for equivariant models on real tasks.

The causal link between measured symmetry breaking and model performance is not established. Many confounders remain, including architecture choice, model capacity, local versus global features, property type, and train/test distribution details.
The comparison between augmentation settings, group averaging, and equivariant baselines is not always apples-to-apples, especially across different architectures and datasets.

The theoretical analysis is interesting but narrow: linear/ridge settings with Gaussian assumptions and stylized covariance models only partially explain the behavior of modern equivariant neural networks.

Reproducibility has issues: the reproducibility statement appears to contain a missing code URL, and many experimental details are pushed to a long appendix, making it difficult to assess whether all results are easily reproducible.
The paper’s claims and recommendations are stronger than the evidence supports. The work is promising and informative, but not yet convincing enough for a clear top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored issue: data distributions can break symmetries even when labels/functions are symmetric, which can change the value of equivariant architectures and augmentation.

The classifier two-sample metric is simple, interpretable, broadly applicable, and validated with useful synthetic controls; the finding that common point-cloud and molecular/materials benchmarks are highly canonicalized is impactful.

The work combines a clean diagnostic, a task-dependent companion metric, ridge-regression theory under asymmetric covariances, and experiments across many datasets including MNIST, ModelNet40, QM9, QM7b, rMD17, OC20, and LLM materials data.
The paper is appropriately nuanced: it does not claim that symmetry breaking always makes equivariance harmful, and the QM9/QM7b versus ModelNet40 contrast is scientifically interesting.
The appendices contain substantial experimental detail, ablations for the main metric, p-value analyses, and model/training specifications.
weaknesses: The main metric is classifier-dependent rather than intrinsic; its value depends on architecture, optimization, sample size, and representation, making cross-dataset comparisons somewhat hard to interpret.

The task-dependent metric is less mature: it depends on a chosen canonicalization network, has acknowledged sensitivity/optimization issues, and lacks a principled threshold for deciding when equivariance will hurt.
The theory is insightful but stylized; linear ridge regression with Gaussian covariates only partially explains modern equivariant neural networks.
Some empirical comparisons could be stronger because equivariant and non-equivariant models differ in architecture family, optimization, and inductive biases despite rough parameter matching.

The downstream story is mixed: high symmetry breaking is found broadly, yet augmentation/equivariance helps on many molecular tasks. The locality and task-relevance explanations are plausible but not fully causal.
The reproducibility statement appears to have a missing public code URL in the manuscript text.
